Il s’est écoulé plus de 102 jours depuis: More than 102 days have passed since the start of Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip, and the victims number in the thousands. On social media and at the demonstrations filling streets around the world, despair is palpable and dialogue is becoming rarer.
Nous avons fait la rencontre de Ronit Ya: We met Ronit Yarosky, a former Canadian-Israeli soldier who decided to commit herself to dialogue. As we learn about her journey, we come to see that dialogue, like faith, is a matter of belief. It is not stable but rather a fluctuating practice, marked by the beauty and the drama of its evolution.

C’est le 18 décembre dernier, trois jour: It is December 18, three days after Hanukkah, when we meet Ronit Yarosky at her home. Christmas lights adorn the streets of NDG, and the cars glisten with raindrops.
Écho de ses origines et de son parcours,: An echo of her origins and her journey, an outpouring of colours and objects steeped in history decorates her living room. Ronit sits comfortably on the couch. A tray adorned with Arabic calligraphy devoted to the divine names, such as Allah, holds pride of place in the middle of the room. She bought it at the souk in Jerusalem a few years ago.
Ronit est née à Montréal et a quitté la: Ronit was born in Montréal and left the city with her family at 14 to settle in Israel.
« Toute ma famille est en Israël ; j’y a: “My whole family is in Israel; I lived there for about 10 years,” she explains.
Arrivée en 1983, sa famille emménage prè: Her family arrived in 1983 and moved to a place near Tel Aviv. Ronit remembers her teenage years: “We took a lot of little trips with the class, with friends. I was actively involved in scouts. The climate there wasn’t too cold, so we could spend most of our time outdoors.”
Ronit Yarosky sur une plage de Tel-Aviv: Ronit Yarosky on a Tel Aviv beach in 1986. Courtesy of Ronit Yarosky.
Après une brève pause, elle ajoute : « C: After a brief pause, she adds: “It was the era of naivety, of ignorance is bliss, it was la vita bella.”
En 1986, Ronit obtient son diplôme d’étu: In 1986, Ronit earned her high school diploma and joined the ranks of the Israeli army to fulfil her national duty. The first Intifada broke out a year later, in December 1987. In her captivating essay The Hole Truth, part of a book titled Beyond Tribal Loyalties: Personal Stories of Jewish Peace Activists, she shares her experience of more than two years during the turbulent period of the Intifada.
« Je savais que les Arabes de Cisjordani: “I knew that the Arabs of the West Bank threw stones and caused trouble, but I didn’t know why and I hardly cared. While I was in the army, we stayed in many Arab towns, all anonymous to me because they were ‘just’ Arab towns and therefore had no importance in my life…” (Free translation, The Hole Truth, p. 121)
Ronit Yarosky en 1986, portant son unifo: Ronit Yarosky in 1986, wearing her IDF soldier’s uniform, a few months before the first Intifada. Courtesy of Ronit Yarosky.
Dans un autre passage, elle se souvient: In another passage, she recalls going to a military police base. There she saw five Palestinian children handcuffed, crouching on the ground, blindfolded. More than an hour later, when Ronit came out, they were still there, in the same position.
Ce souvenir l’a hantée pendant des année: That memory haunted her for years. “I realized that I had walked past those children without seeing them, as if they were chairs. I had noticed them the same way I would have noticed a piece of furniture.” (Free translation, The Hole Truth, p. 124)
Elle confie : « J’étais fière. J’ai beau: She confides: “I was proud. I loved that period of military service, I learned a lot of useful things, but it was also done in ignorance. It was just normal, it’s what you did at 18: you become a soldier, you don’t ask questions.”
Dans son essai, elle se souvient en trai: In her essay, she recalls standing in front of the Israeli flag and singing the national anthem:
« Des larmes coulaient sur mon visage, j: “Tears were streaming down my face, I couldn’t imagine anything more incredible and moving than serving my country and singing Hatikva as a soldier. I saw nothing abnormal in this situation – a soldier singing her national anthem, but on occupied land.” (Free translation, The Hole Truth, p. 123)
Avec le recul, elle se questionne sur la: Looking back, she wonders about the source of that “ignorance.” “Maybe it’s the fact that I hadn’t always lived in Israel, and so I didn’t know what questions to ask or what information I was missing. Or maybe it’s linked to the way history and national and cultural myths are told. Maybe it’s a mix of both.”
Elle évoque ce qu’elle appelle un « myth: She brings up what she calls a “national myth”: “We grew up with it: a land without a people, for a people without a land. And we truly believed that! But it wasn’t an empty land. It’s not easy for a human being to realize and accept that they are there because of something wrong or unjust.”

À l’âge de 27 ans, Ronit revient à Montr: At 27, Ronit returned to Montréal to pursue a master’s degree at McGill University. While researching her thesis, she came across Benny Morris’s book Birth of the Palestinian Problem. “As I was leafing through it, I spotted the name of my uncle’s village [a place called Ijzim before 1948, not Kerem Maharal as it is today]. I was completely shocked. Shocked!” she repeats, raising her voice.
Elle réalise alors subitement que ce vil: She suddenly realized that the village had existed before her uncle arrived. Talking with her mother, she learned that the Nakba – the Arabic term meaning “catastrophe” that refers to the 1948 Palestinian exodus – was a known historical episode in her family. In fact, her uncle still avoids talking about it.
Cette découverte l’incite à explorer dav: The discovery pushed her to explore this history further. “I started very slowly. I read, I met Palestinians. It was the first time I was intentionally talking with Palestinians. I remember the first time in my life that I said the word ‘Palestine.’ I felt very brave, because at the time in Israel, you couldn’t say that word,” Ronit remembers.
« J’ai vécu avec une histoire remplie de: “I lived with a history full of lies,” she says, shaking her head.
En 2000, trois ans après la fin de sa ma: In 2000, three years after finishing her master’s, she returned to Israel because her father had fallen ill. Two months after she got back, in September, the second Intifada broke out. This time, Ronit played a completely different role. “I became truly an activist, I took part in the demonstrations [in the occupied territories] for human rights.”

Elle relate cette expérience dans son es: She recounts that experience in her essay The Hole Truth:
« Je me souviens d’une fois où l’armée n: “I remember one time when the army was firing tear gas at us, and the Palestinians offered us shelter. I thought: ‘It’s my army attacking me, and my “enemy” helping me!’ Seeing (really seeing – not like when I was a soldier and was ‘blind’) the soldiers’ behaviour for the first time was revealing. How can we treat people this way? Maybe we don’t really think they are people. Not as much as we are.” (Free translation, The Hole Truth, p. 123)
Elle décrit cette période comme ayant ét: She describes that period as particularly difficult, since some members of her family, friends and neighbours in Israel did not look kindly on her activism. She was often called a “radical leftist,” a label she never liked. Since then, her uncle and a few of her cousins have refused to speak to her.
De retour à Montréal, une question la ta: Back in Montréal, one question nagged at her: how could the Israeli state coexist with a Palestinian state? “I said we have to talk to each other. If we can’t do it here in Canada, over there they don’t stand a chance! It was even a kind of obligation, to be an example, a leader. After all, we’re in Canada, we have multiculturalism,” she says, shrugging.
Ronit s’implique donc dans des groupes c: Ronit got involved in groups such as the <l1>Palestinian and Jewish United (PAJU</l1>) and <l2>Women in Black</l2>, but something was missing. “The problem with these groups is that you don’t manage to reach the people who need to hear other points of view. Generally, when you’re a member of these groups, you already see the reality of the occupation. You’re preaching to the converted.”
Après une gorgée d’eau, elle replonge da: After a sip of water, she dives back into her memories of the early 2000s. “Every Friday, there was a demonstration in front of the Consulate General of Israel in Montréal, and often there was a counter-demonstration. I kept thinking: ‘Where can I go, since choosing the Palestinians’ side means being anti-Israel? And if I stand with the Israelis, it means being anti-Palestine. But I’m neither. I’m for this and for that.’” she says.
Ronit Yarosky n’était pas la seule à êtr: Ronit Yarosky was not the only one who felt torn. So, with her Palestinian friend Nada Sefian, she founded the Groupe Dialogue Montréal (GDM) in 2003. “We wanted to create learning opportunities, safe spaces to listen to each other and share our stories without giving up our initial beliefs.”
Elle désigne son salon et poursuit: « C’: She points to her living room and continues: “This is where we held our first meeting, before we founded the group. There were about forty of us, gathered to watch a film. There was strong demand for this kind of activity. People wanted a space to talk.”
Le regard de Ronit s’éloigne, elle pense: Ronit’s gaze drifts; she is thinking about the current situation. “In a war, you want to know the enemy to find their weaknesses, but in dialogue, you want to know the other to find their strengths, their humanity. All it takes is a small crack in our inner wall [to recognize] that there’s a small possibility that we need to question ourselves.”
Ronit se redresse et soupire : « Je cons: Ronit straightens up and sighs: “I consider myself lucky, because it’s not simple or easy to find that willingness to question. In my case, and that of many Jewish people, for example, if you say ‘A land without a people, for a people without a land,’ there’s nothing to question. It’s treated as a fact. If no one told you, if you never read or heard it, how are you supposed to know?” She also stresses that it is as hard to step out of one’s convictions as it is to keep questioning. Dialogue is thus a long-term commitment.

Cet engagement envers le dialogue s’est: That commitment to dialogue collapsed, however, in the aftermath of October 7, 2023. Ronit Yarosky, who had long believed in the two-state solution and the transformative power of dialogue, finds herself at a crossroads.
Le 6 octobre déjà le son des sirènes rés: As early as October 6, the sound of sirens rang out on Ronit’s phone, sowing panic, though she hadn’t heard an alert since 2021. Rockets had been fired near Tel Aviv, where her family lives. After making sure her loved ones were safe in the bomb shelter, she fell asleep. On waking, she discovered the scale of the Hamas attack and immediately contacted her family. “For me, it was as shocking as when I discovered that the Nakba had happened,” she says.
Incrédule face aux images, elle communiq: Incredulous at the images, she contacted a friend of Middle Eastern origin in Montréal, hoping to hear some reassuring words. But he set about justifying armed resistance under an occupation regime, which left her perplexed. She remembers: “Yes, maybe you’re right, but right now, do you have nothing else to say to me? Don’t you have even a small gesture of compassion to share?” As she speaks, she makes a gesture as if holding a grain.
« La compassion n’est pas comme un gâtea: “Compassion isn’t like a cake. If I give you some, there’s no less left for me – there’s enough for everyone. This is a 20-year relationship that I have to call into question. After all these years of dialogue, I ask myself: ‘Does it mean nothing at all? Or is dialogue valid only if I criticize the State of Israel?’”

En novembre 2023, un mois après le début: In November 2023, a month after the start of Israel’s war on Gaza, Ronit boarded a plane to be with her family: “My heart remains in Israel, it stays Israeli.”
Entourée de sa famille, de ses amis et d: Surrounded by her family, friends and neighbours, she was asked the same question by everyone: “So tell me, all those friends you supported for years, did they contact you to say something on October 7?” Dejected, she admits: “Unfortunately, I had no answer to give them other than no.”
Selon Ronit, Il y a eu une brève période: According to Ronit, there was a brief window in which to offer compassion to Israelis, but the train has gone by, and the situation is not improving. “It’s not easy to see what happened in Israel and, of course, what is happening in Gaza,” she confides.
Malgré la confusion, certaines questions: Despite the confusion, some questions have become clearer for our interviewee: “Now, I understand the importance of the IDF, and also the importance of a safe Israeli place in a world that takes us in.”
En Israël, la tension est palpable : « T: In Israel, the tension is palpable: “Everyone is constantly glued to the news, 24 hours a day. Even those who were on the left are retreating. Everyone is in their own bubble, in their own corner, ready to fight, to protect themselves. In general, even outside Israel, opinions – even though I don’t like using this word – have become radicalized. They lose all nuance. But everything is a matter of nuance.”
Au moment de notre rencontre avec Ronit,: By the time we met Ronit, the war was entering its third month. The Montrealer, paradoxically, feels safer in Israel than outside the country. “Right now, my main concern is my return to Montréal, with the rise of antisemitism. This fear is new to me. I don’t know what to do with these emotions. I realize I have fewer and fewer answers when it comes to the Israeli-Palestinian situation.”
« Est-ce que je crois toujours au dialog: “Do I still believe in dialogue? Yes. But do I believe in dialogue today, right now? No,” says Ronit.
« Ç’a été une énorme partie de ma vie. C: “It was an enormous part of my life. It was a priority for me, but it feels like we’ll have to start over from zero, like on day one. Those 25 years of work in dialogue seem wasted, and I don’t know what to make of it.”
« Les émotions sont trop fortes. On est: “Emotions are too strong. We’re in the middle of a war, each in our own corner. We only have compassion for ourselves. Israel is a country in mourning. The Palestinians are a nation in mourning,” she says softly.
Elle soupire et continue : « Quand le te: She sighs and continues: “When the time is right, each of the two sides will have to take responsibility and approach the situation honestly. We have to put our cards on the table and say: ‘This is what I did.’ We have to start talking to each other again. I tell myself it may take another generation to restart the process.”
Le silence s’installe dans le salon, pon: Silence settles over the living room, punctuated by the sound of the rain picking up its rhythm again. Ronit looks out the window and concludes: “In spite of everything, I keep hope, I still believe in dialogue, in our capacity for empathy.”
